newsitem.title: USA: Intel warning sends stock sharply lower.
newsitem.headline: Intel warning sends stock sharply lower.

text.p: Intel Corp. , the leading maker of computer chips and a technology bellwether, stunned Wall Street Friday by warning that its second-quarter revenue and profit will fall short of expectations.

Intel, which consistently has managed to exceed Wall Street's expectations quarter after quarter, said revenue for the period is expected to drop 5 percent to 10 percent below the first quarter's $6.4 billion, due mostly to weaker sales in Europe.
Gross margin, a key measure of profitability, also could be under the first-quarter's level of 64 percent.
The warning raised concern on Wall Street that worldwide demand for computers, the world's third-largest industry, could be slowing.

"I'm in Taiwan at the moment and (PC assemblers) are saying that business is weak," said Drew Peck, analyst at investment bank Cowen & Co. "That would suggest Europe is not alone. The PC market has lulled a bit."

Intel's stock tumbled more than 14 percent to $137.875 on the news before recovering somewhat to $152.75, down $11.02 in a frenzied Nasdaq market. More than 45 million shares changed hand, making it the most active stock in U.S. trading.

The sell-off quickly spread to other technology stocks. International Business Machines Corp. fell $3.125 to $84.75 on the New York Stock Exchange. Microsoft Corp. slid as much as $8.375 to $117.50 on Nasdaq.

The Dow Jones industrial average was also hit hard, falling 84 points to 7,246 before recovering most of the loss to stand at 7,314, down 15 points, at midday. The technology-heavy Nasdaq index was down 12.47 at 1,390.57, but well up from the 47-point fall it suffered at the opening.
"This is a bellwether event," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.

In a terse news release, Intel, based in Santa Clara, Calif., said European sales were weaker than expected. But it said there was "strong demand" for the new Pentium II chip and chips with MMX multimedia technology.

Some analysts said Intel's problem is not slowing PC demand. Instead, they said, the company cannot make enough of the new chips. First-tier PC makers, such as Compaq Computer Corp., are reluctant to order Intel's older chips.

"It's a one-quarter problem," said Dan Niles, analyst at Robertson Stephens & Co. in New York, who kept his buy rating on Intel. Only the second-tier PC makers, mostly in Europe and Asia, are experiencing slowing demand because they cannot get Intel's jazzier chips, Niles said.
Compaq, which is among the first to get its hands on new Intel chips, said Friday it has had a good quarter so far.

"Our order growth is well above that of the marketplace," said Compaq Chief Financial Officer Earl Mason. "We feel very good about the quarter and feel very bullish about the outlook for the rest of the year."
Still, Intel faces serious competition for the first time in a long time.
On Friday, Cyrix Corp. introduced its latest challenge to Intel's domination of the PC industry with a processor that will compete with the Pentium II at half the price.
"We think this is the year of the alternative processor," said Stan Swearington, a director of product marketing at Cyrix in Richardson, Texas.

Cyrix said its new processor will be priced at $190 for the 166-megahertz version, $240 for the 200-megahertz chip and $320 for its fastest, at 233 megahertz, in quantities of 1,000. A 266-megahertz model is expected in the fourth quarter.
The lower-speed chips will compete with Intel's Pentium MMX chips.

IBM said Friday it will manufacture Cyrix's new Pentium-compatible chip and will market an IBM-branded version. IBM said its IBM 6x86MX is fully compatible with the newest series of Pentium chips and comes in three versions: the PR166, PR200 and PR233.
All three incorporate MMX technology -- multimedia instructions added to the chip architecture.
Cowen & Co.'s Peck said the new competition has forced Intel to cut its prices on its chips, lowering its gross margins and profits.
Intel said second-quarter gross margins were expected to be 60 percent "plus or minus a few points."
Over the long term, the company said, it expected its gross margin percentage "will be 50 percent plus or minus a few points," in line with previous company forecasts.
In the second quarter of 1996, Intel reported a profit of $1.04 billion, or $1.17 a share, on revenues of $4.62 billion.
Prior to the company's outlook statement, analysts had expected Intel to report a second-quarter profit of $2.16 per share, according to a consensus of 35 analysts compiled by the First Call service.
Intel also said second-quarter expenses are expected to be 7 percent to 9 percent above the $1.3 billion it recorded in the prior quarter, mostly to increase production of its new chips.
